issues.legal_issue: Omitting citation in the district where property is situated does not by itself make probate proceedings defective in substance when the omission did not prejudice an interested person in the circumstances.
material_facts: The probate applicant, the testator, and the family lived where the probate proceedings were conducted, although the property was situated in another district.
The person seeking revocation was a minor living with the probate applicant when probate was sought.
She did not establish that citation in the property district would have brought the proceedings to her attention or otherwise benefited her, or that the omission caused prejudice.
The will remained unchallenged, and she waited many years before seeking revocation.
issues.conclusion: The omission of citation in the district where the property was situated was, in these circumstances, a procedural irregularity and not a defect in substance constituting just cause to revoke probate.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 263 of the Indian Succession Act, a grant may be revoked for just cause, including proceedings defective in substance. A defect is substantial when it substantially affects the regularity and correctness of the prior proceedings; omission of citation is not an absolute ground for revocation irrespective of the circumstances. The Court applied Anil Behari Ghoshe v. Smt. Latika Bala Dassi, AIR 1955 SC 566, which recognizes that absence of citation may be a ground for revocation where the omitted person could have entered a caveat, but that the court must exercise judicial discretion on the proved facts. The Court also discussed Mt. Sheopati Kuer v. Ramakant Dikshit and other cases concerning representation of minors, distinguishing cases where a minor's interests were at stake or were not effectively represented.

rule.if: probate_revocation_proceeding and citation_omitted_in_property_district and parties_resided_elsewhere and claimant_would_not_have_benefited_from_local_citation and no_evidence_of_prejudice and will_remained_unchallenged

predicates.probate_revocation_proceeding: A person sought revocation of a grant of probate.
predicates.citation_omitted_in_property_district: The probate court did not issue citation in the district where the estate property was situated.
predicates.parties_resided_elsewhere: The testator, the probate applicant, and the person seeking revocation lived in another place connected with the proceedings.
predicates.claimant_would_not_have_benefited_from_l: The person seeking revocation would not have gained notice or other benefit from citation being issued in the property district.
predicates.no_evidence_of_prejudice: The person seeking revocation did not produce evidence that the citation omission prejudiced them.
predicates.will_remained_unchallenged: The person seeking revocation did not establish a challenge to the will's validity.

issues.definition: When a probate revocation proceeding involves an omitted local citation but the claimant would not have benefited from it, no prejudice is shown, and the will remains unchallenged, the omission is not a substantial defect justifying revocation.

issues.legal_issue: An allegation that probate was obtained by fraud does not establish just cause for revocation without specific particulars and supporting evidence.
material_facts: The person seeking revocation alleged that the will and grant resulted from fraud and undue influence.
She did not plead specific particulars of the alleged fraud or undue influence and did not adduce evidence to prove them.
The signature on the will and its genuineness were not challenged.
issues.conclusion: The fraud allegation did not establish just cause to revoke probate because it was neither specifically pleaded nor proved.
issues.legal_principle: Section 263(b) of the Indian Succession Act treats a grant obtained fraudulently by a false suggestion or concealment of material matters as just cause for revocation. A party alleging fraud must plead its full particulars, and the case must be decided on those particulars; general allegations are insufficient. The allegation must also be supported by evidence.

rule.if: probate_revocation_proceeding and fraud_alleged_as_ground_for_revocation and fraud_particulars_not_pleaded and no_evidence_proving_fraud and will_genuineness_not_challenged

predicates.probate_revocation_proceeding: A person sought revocation of a grant of probate.
predicates.fraud_alleged_as_ground_for_revocation: The person seeking revocation claimed that the grant had been obtained by fraud.
predicates.fraud_particulars_not_pleaded: The person seeking revocation did not set out specific particulars of the alleged fraud.
predicates.no_evidence_proving_fraud: The person seeking revocation did not produce evidence establishing the alleged fraud.
predicates.will_genuineness_not_challenged: The person seeking revocation did not challenge the authenticity of the will.

issues.definition: In a probate revocation proceeding, a fraud allegation that lacks pleaded particulars and supporting evidence, where the will's genuineness is unchallenged, does not establish just cause for revocation.

issues.legal_issue: The limitation period for an application to revoke probate is governed by the general three-year period for applications to a civil court, and, where the applicant was a minor when probate was granted, time runs from attaining majority.
material_facts: The applicant was a minor when probate was granted and attained majority later.
She applied to revoke probate decades after attaining majority, well beyond three years, and offered no acceptable explanation for the delay.
The grant of probate had not been successfully challenged in the intervening period.
issues.conclusion: The application for revocation was barred by limitation; because the applicant was a minor when probate was granted, the limitation period began when she attained majority, and she did not apply within three years thereafter.
issues.legal_principle: Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, applies to applications made to a civil court under any Act and prescribes three years from when the right to apply accrues. The Court relied on Kerala State Electricity Board, Trivandrum v. T.P. Kunhaliumma, AIR 1997 SC 282, Krishna Kumar Sharma v. Rajesh Kumar Sharma, (2009) 11 SCC 537, and Kunvarjeet Singh Khandpur v. Kirandeep Kaur, (2008) 8 SCC 463. A probate operates as a judgment in rem; for an applicant who was a minor when probate was granted, the Court held that the limitation period runs from the date the applicant attains majority.

rule.if: probate_revocation_application and claimant_was_minor_when_probate_granted and application_filed_more_than_three_years_after_majority and no_acceptable_delay_explanation

predicates.probate_revocation_application: A person applied to a civil court to revoke a grant of probate.
predicates.claimant_was_minor_when_probate_granted: The person seeking revocation was a minor when probate was granted.
predicates.application_filed_more_than_three_years_: The person seeking revocation applied more than three years after attaining adulthood.
predicates.no_acceptable_delay_explanation: The person seeking revocation did not provide an acceptable explanation for the delay.

issues.definition: A probate revocation application is time-barred when the applicant was a minor at the grant, applies more than three years after attaining adulthood, and provides no acceptable explanation for the delay.

issues.legal_issue: The distinction between common-form and solemn-form probate does not bar a challenge to probate in India, and the distinction is immaterial where the grant followed judicial consideration and the challenge is adjudicated through revocation proceedings.
material_facts: The probate court recorded evidence and published citation before granting probate.
The person seeking revocation later applied to the court under the statutory revocation procedure, and that application was adjudicated through the courts.
She argued that the grant had been made in common form rather than solemn form.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that India has no common-form probate system; the grant was in solemn form, and the distinction raised no obstacle to the revocation challenge, making the argument academic.
issues.legal_principle: The Indian probate system involves judicial determination, unlike the English common-form procedure described in the argument. The Court relied on Southern Bank Ltd. v. Kesardeo Ganeriwalla, AIR 1958 Cal 377, and held that Section 263 of the Indian Succession Act permits a person to seek revocation for just cause, with the application subject to judicial adjudication.

rule.if: probate_grant_proceeding and grant_followed_judicial_consideration and evidence_recorded_before_grant and citation_published and revocation_challenge_adjudicated_by_court

predicates.probate_grant_proceeding: A person sought a grant of probate from a court.
predicates.grant_followed_judicial_consideration: The court considered the matter before granting probate.
predicates.evidence_recorded_before_grant: The court recorded evidence before granting probate.
predicates.citation_published: The court published citation in connection with the probate proceedings.
predicates.revocation_challenge_adjudicated_by_cour: A later application challenging the grant was considered and adjudicated by a court.

issues.definition: When probate follows judicial consideration, evidence, and published citation, and a later challenge is judicially adjudicated, the common-form distinction does not bar that challenge.
